def count_self_supporting(n, m):
    """Count the self-supporting arrays of length n over the alphabet {1, ..., m}.

    An array (a_1, ..., a_n) with each a_i an integer in {1, ..., m} is called
    *self-supporting* if every value that occurs in it occurs at least that
    many times: for every integer v, the number of indices i with a_i == v is
    either 0 or at least v. (So the value 3 may only appear if it appears at
    least 3 times; the value 1 may appear any positive number of times.)

    Arrays are ordered sequences: two arrays that differ in any position are
    counted as different.

    Input domain: n and m are integers with 1 <= n <= 100 and 1 <= m <= 100.

    Returns the exact number of self-supporting arrays as a Python int (the
    count can far exceed 64 bits; no modulus is applied).

    Edge cases implied by the definition: any value v > n can never occur in a
    valid array (it cannot reach v copies), so the answer for (n, m) equals
    the answer for (n, min(n, m)); if m == 1 the answer is 1 (the all-ones
    array). There are no ties to break; the output is a single integer.

    >>> count_self_supporting(3, 2)
    5
    >>> count_self_supporting(4, 3)
    17
    >>> count_self_supporting(1, 5)
    1
    """
